knowledge_point.title: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Non-Closed Curve

question.:question/problem:
![](images/c7/c71395cfe5877546509f24656ba23f0883cbd3ee8c145c10abae9600c8bd5c4a.png)

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=x\,i+y\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j$ for $t\in [0,1],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](images/e9/e90c36e34c6ab51f15707685a22c8bd2c749b9857ca24c59631f09dfbda495c6.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y={t}^{2}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=t, \\ Q(x,y) & =y={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t)\cdot (2t)-({t}^{2})\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

The curve $C$ is given by ${y}^{2}=4x$ from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(1,2).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=2\,i-4\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2},\,y=t,\,t\in [0,2].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(1,2.)$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/b7/b7ac1ce4a79528f5660b8f898739da72489ebe8e8fc156020efae77a103fbec4.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =2, \\ Q(x,y) & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2})=\frac{1}{2}t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2)\cdot (1)-(-4)\cdot (\frac{1}{2}t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2+2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(2t+{t}^{2}){|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(2\cdot 2+{2}^{2})-0 \\  & =8\end{aligned}

The curve $C$ is given by $x=-\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ from the point $(1,\frac{1}{e})$ to the point $(0,1).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=2{y}^{2}\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,y=t,\,t\in [\frac{1}{e},1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(1,\frac{1}{e})$ to the point $(0,1).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/08/08fc4561a322b690da7bd28a9e69a91c687256e8a902ec7690dda5e6a1c689a6.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =0, \\ Q(x,y) & =2{y}^{2}=2{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{ln}⁡t)=-\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/e}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/e}^{1}(0)\cdot (1)-(2{t}^{2})\cdot (-\frac{1}{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/e}^{1}2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =({t}^{2}){|}_{1/e}^{1} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The curve $C$ is given by $x={e}^{y}$ from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(e,1).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{2}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={e}^{t}\,y=t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(e,1).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/ba/ba6285008fd90835fdbf73203b76a0a01d713889d9939979aaec54bebd0a8c49.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}={t}^{2}, \\ Q(x,y) & =\frac{1}{x}={e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2})\cdot (1)-({e}^{-t})\cdot ({e}^{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-1)-0 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=\frac{1}{t},\,t\in [\frac{1}{2},2].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(\frac{1}{2},2)$ to the point $(2,\frac{1}{2}).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/cc/cc9d66f800a57f27673577cd3fd179b4cd6ff64585c5dc1a867317d8d592e485.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={x}^{2}y=t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-y=-\frac{1}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})=-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(t)\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})-(-\frac{1}{t})\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}0\,\text{d}t \\  & =0\end{aligned}
